intro:
This track is about what we want from a program that keeps data, and how to tell whether it delivers. Most lessons follow one small company: it runs the program that records card payments for a café and other shops, and keeps a running balance for each one. Every lesson starts from a scene in that world, or from an app you use every day, and builds the idea up from there, with real numbers from published systems and outages.

By the end, you can describe any data system in the words the rest of the course uses. You'll know which data is the official record and which is a copy worked out from it, and whether a question is a quick lookup or one that reads years of history. You'll be able to say how fast it answers, in percentiles rather than averages, and which breakages it survives. You'll know what its load is and which extreme of that load breaks it, what its machines share as it grows, and what it costs the people who run it.

The six lessons:

1. What a data system is: records, derived data and two kinds of work
2. Latency, percentiles and the tail
3. Faults, failures and the people who run systems
4. Describing load: the home timeline
5. Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud
6. Systems people can live with: operability, simplicity and change

You need to read a little code, such as a loop, a function and a class, and nothing else. No background in networks, operating systems or databases is assumed: every term is explained the first time it appears. The next two tracks, Computer networking and Operating systems, go one layer down, to the machinery that every number in this track rests on.

The labs are small programs in Kotlin, a language much like Java but shorter. They live in the `sim` module, one package per lesson (`sfz.found.l01` to `sfz.found.l06`), and need nothing else installed. They model each idea in memory. Where time matters, they use a pretend clock that the code moves forward instead of waiting. So a day of traffic or a three-day alarm window runs in milliseconds, and every test gives the same numbers on every laptop. From the `labs` folder, run `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.found.lNN.*'` until it passes. (`./gradlew` runs Gradle, the tool that builds and tests the labs.) `./gradlew :sim:solutionTest --tests 'sfz.found.lNN.*'` runs the same tests against the finished answers. The Try its run small demos with `./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=<class> --console=plain -q`.
cheatsheet:
## Words this track defines

| Term | Meaning | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| System of record | the one place that holds the official version of each fact; it wins every disagreement | 1 |
| Derived data | anything worked out from the record (an index, a cache, a stored total, a report); it can be thrown away and rebuilt | 1 |
| Index, cache, queue, batch job | a lookup table from a key to its record; a saved copy of a costly answer; a list of jobs waiting to be done; a program that works through a big pile of input in one run | 1 |
| Operational and analytical work (OLTP, OLAP) | a few records found by key, in milliseconds, for the app; millions of records read, in seconds or minutes, for people asking new questions | 1 |
| Response time, service time | how long the person or program asking waits, from start to end; the part of it spent working on the request | 2 |
| Percentile (p50, p99) | the time that 50 or 99 requests in 100 beat; combine histograms (counts of requests in each range of times), never average percentiles | 2 |
| Coordinated omission | a speed test that waits for each answer before sending the next, so it stops sending during a stall and the stall barely shows | 2 |
| SLO, error budget, burn rate | a target such as "99.9% of payments succeed over 30 days"; the failures that target allows; how fast they're being used up | 2, 6 |
| Fault, failure | one part goes wrong; the whole service misses its promise | 3 |
| Gray failure | a part that looks healthy to its own checks but is broken for the people using it | 3 |
| Metastable failure | an overload that the system's own retries keep going after the cause has gone | 3 |
| Load parameter | a number that drives a system's cost: a rate, a size, a ratio or a count per key | 4 |
| Fan-out on read, on write | build the answer when someone reads it; copy each new item to every reader when it's written | 4 |
| Celebrity problem | one key so big (an account with millions of followers, a very busy shop) that its work holds up everyone else's | 4 |
| Scaling up, scaling out | one bigger machine; more machines | 5 |
| Shared memory, disk, nothing | what the workers in a group of machines share: one machine's memory; the storage; only the network | 5 |
| COST | how much hardware a system needs before it beats one well-written program on one thread | 5 |
| Essential, accidental complexity | complexity that comes from the problem; complexity that comes from how the system was built | 6 |
| Expand and contract | change stored data in small steps that can each be undone: add the new form, move to it, then remove the old one | 6 |

## Formulas

```text
average response time, one worker   S / (1 - busy share)              10 ms of work: 20 ms at 50% busy, 100 ms at 90%
Little's law                        in progress = rate x time         2,000 a second x 50 ms = 100 requests in progress
waiting for N answers at once       P(slow) = 1 - (1 - p)^N           p = 1%, N = 100: 63%; N = 200: 87%
Amdahl's law                        speed-up = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / N)  never more than 1 / s
Universal Scalability Law           N / (1 + a(N - 1) + bN(N - 1))    peaks at sqrt((1 - a) / b) workers
fan-out on write vs on read         posts x followers vs reads x followers: the follower count cancels
celebrity threshold                 fan-out writes per second x delivery deadline
error budget, in minutes            (1 - SLO) x days x 1,440
burn rate                           share of requests failing / (1 - SLO)
budget spent                        burn rate x minutes / (days x 1,440)
programs called one after another   multiply their success rates: 0.999^3 = 99.7%
```

S is the work on one request (its service time), and p is the chance that one answer is slow. In Amdahl's law, s is the share of the job that can't be split, and N is the number of workers. In the Universal Scalability Law, a (alpha) is the time spent waiting for something only one worker can use at a time, and b (beta) is the cost of every pair of workers keeping in step.

## Numbers worth remembering

| What | Value | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999% over 30 days | allow 43.2 min, 4.32 min, 26 s of complete outage | 2 |
| Burn-rate alarms for a 30-day target | page someone (send an alert that wakes them) at 14.4 over 1 hour and 5 minutes (2% of the budget gone); page at 6 over 6 hours and 30 minutes (5%); open a ticket at 1 over 3 days and 6 hours (10%) | 2, 6 |
| Hard drives failing | 1.36% a year (Backblaze, 2025): 10,000 drives lose one every 2 or 3 days | 3 |
| Worst failures caused by error-handling code | 92% of those studied (Yuan and colleagues, 2014) | 3 |
| Twitter, 2012 | about 300,000 timeline reads and 5,000 posts a second, 800 posts per ready-made timeline; one post to 31 million followers took up to 5 minutes | 4 |
| Bluesky, 2025 | a user gets `min(2000 / follows, 1)` of their timeline writes | 4 |
| Largest machine you can rent from AWS | 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory (`u7inh-32tb.480xlarge`) | 5 |
| Aurora storage | 10 GB segments, 6 copies in 3 zones; a write needs 4 copies and a read 3; a lost segment is copied again in about 10 s | 5 |
| COST paper (a Twitter follower network) | one thread on a laptop with union-find: 15 s; published systems on 128 cores: 251 to 1,784 s | 5 |
| AWS traffic between zones | $0.02 per GiB, the reason Kafka (a program that keeps logs of messages) added diskless topics (KIP-1150) | 5, 6 |
| 37signals leaving S3 | about $1.5M a year for S3, against $1.5M of storage hardware plus under $200K a year to run it (the company's own figures) | 6 |

## Questions to ask of any data system

1. Which store is the system of record, and what is worked out from it? Could you rebuild every copy? (lesson 1)
2. What are its p50, p99 and p99.9 response times, measured where the user waits, by a test that sends on a fixed schedule? (lesson 2)
3. Which faults does it survive, do they strike one part at a time, and what do retries do to it when it's overloaded? (lesson 3)
4. What are its load parameters, and which extreme (a celebrity, a heavy follower, a very busy shop) dominates the cost? (lesson 4)
5. What do its machines share, where is the copy that survives a crash, and what is only a cache? (lesson 5)
6. Does it beat one good thread on one big machine? (lesson 5)
7. What is its target (SLO), do its alarms ring on burn rate, and can each change be undone? (lesson 6)
recap: Every data system has a system of record, where each fact is written first and once, and it wins every disagreement. Indexes, caches, stored totals and warehouses are worked out from it and can be thrown away and rebuilt. Quick lookups for the app and big reads of history for people belong on different copies.

A request's response time is the work on it plus the waiting. The waiting grows very fast as a worker gets busy: 10 ms of work takes 100 ms on average at 90% busy. Report percentiles, combine histograms instead of averaging percentiles, and test speed by sending on a fixed schedule.

When one screen waits for many answers, a rare slow answer becomes the normal case: with 100 answers that are each slow 1% of the time, 63% of screens are slow. A target with an error budget turns the slow and failed requests into a promise.

A fault is one part going wrong; a failure is the service missing its promise. Hardware faults are routine and mostly strike one part at a time, so copies help. Bugs, settings and changes by people strike everywhere at once and cause the big outages, and retries without a budget can keep an overload going after its cause has gone.

Describe load with the numbers that drive cost, as a spread up to the maximum. Preparing each feed in advance wins whenever reads outnumber posts, until one celebrity or heavy follower breaks it, so real feeds mix both designs.

Growing past one machine means choosing what the machines share: memory, disk or nothing. The Universal Scalability Law shows where workers wait and what they must keep in agreement; past its peak, more workers make the job slower.

Cloud databases keep the lasting copy of the data on separate storage machines and treat the computers that run the database as replaceable, so always ask where the durable copy is. Measure COST before you spread a job out: many published systems needed hundreds of cores to beat one thread.

Systems live for years. Make them easy to run, keep only the complexity the problem needs, make every change easy to undo, and page people on how fast the error budget burns. Whether to rent machines or own them depends on how much the load varies and on the skills you have.
The limit: every number in this track rests on the network and the operating system underneath, which the next two tracks open up.

quiz.q: Each night, a program works out each shop's daily totals from the payment log and saves them in a table that the shop owners' screen reads. For one shop, the totals table and the log disagree. What do you do?
options: Change the log entries to match the totals
Rebuild that shop's totals from the log
Keep both and show the average
Delete the log entries the totals don't include
quiz.why: The log is the system of record and wins every disagreement. The totals are derived data, so a total that disagrees with the log is out of date or wrong, and rebuilding it from the log fixes it. Changing the record to match a copy destroys the only version you can trust.

quiz.q: A program spends 10 ms of work on each request. Requests arrive at random moments and need different amounts of work, and the program is busy 90% of the time. About how long does a request take on average, waiting included?
options: 11 ms
19 ms
100 ms
1 s
quiz.why: For one worker, the average response time is S / (1 − busy share), where S is the work on one request: 10 ms / 0.1 = 100 ms. Nine tenths of it is waiting in line. 11 ms assumes that being 90% busy adds only a little. 1 s is what you get at 99% busy.

quiz.q: Two copies of the payments program each answer half of the requests. Their p99s, the times that 99 requests in 100 beat, are 40 ms and 400 ms. What is the p99 of the whole service?
options: 220 ms, the average of the two
400 ms, the worse of the two
40 ms, the better of the two
It can't be worked out from the two p99s: add up the two copies' histograms and read the p99 from the total
quiz.why: A percentile depends on the whole spread of times. Here only 0.5% of all requests (half of the slow copy's slowest 1%) take longer than 400 ms, so the overall p99 is below 400 ms, but where depends on both copies' spreads. An average of percentiles is a number with no meaning. A histogram counts the requests in each range of times, and adding the two and reading the p99 from the total gives the right answer.

quiz.q: A new settings file goes out to every computer at once, and within a minute every one of them has crashed. What kind of fault is this, and what protects against it?
options: A correlated settings fault: roll changes out in stages, and have each program check what it receives
An independent hardware fault: add more copies
A gray failure: make health checks follow real requests
A metastable failure: add a retry budget
quiz.why: Every computer got the same bad input at the same moment, so the copies failed together. That's a correlated fault, one that hits many parts at once, and extra copies don't help. Rolling out in stages limits how many computers a bad change reaches before someone notices. A program that checks each new file, and keeps the last good one, stops it at each computer. More copies only add more computers to crash.

quiz.q: The database has a 30-second hiccup and then recovers at once, yet the payments program stays overloaded for an hour. Every time a request takes too long, the program that sent it tries again at once, up to three times. What is going on, and what helps most?
options: The database is still slow: add copies of it for reading
Coordinated omission is hiding the recovery from the graphs
A metastable failure kept going by retries: cap retries with a budget, and drop work nobody is waiting for
A gray failure: fix the health checks
quiz.why: The hiccup made requests time out, and each timeout became up to three more requests. So the work coming in stayed above what the program could handle long after the cause had gone. Waiting longer between retries (backoff) only spreads them out. A retry budget caps how many there are, and dropping work whose senders have given up lets the program catch up.

quiz.q: For the average account on a social network, why does preparing each feed in advance (fan-out on write) do less total work than building it when it's read (fan-out on read)?
options: Writes are cheaper than reads on every database
Feeds are read far more often than accounts post, and for each author the follower count cancels out
The average account has few followers
Fan-out on write skips followers who are offline
quiz.why: Fan-out on write costs one write per follower for each post. Fan-out on read costs one lookup of the author's list for each read by each follower. The follower count is on both sides, so what decides is posts against reads, and reads win by a wide margin (Twitter served about 60 timeline reads for every post in 2012). Few followers makes both designs cheap, so it doesn't explain the difference.

quiz.q: Bluesky's 2025 rule gives a user `min(2000 / follows, 1)` of their timeline writes: 2,000 divided by the number of accounts they follow, but never more than all of them. A user follows 5,000 accounts. What happens?
options: Every post arrives, only later
Only posts from the 2,000 most popular accounts they follow arrive
60% of the posts arrive
About 40% of the posts from the accounts they follow are written into their timeline, and the rest are dropped on purpose
quiz.why: 2,000 / 5,000 = 0.4, so each post lands in this user's timeline with a chance of 0.4, spread across all 5,000 accounts. Nothing is delayed, and popularity doesn't decide which posts are kept. The writes are dropped because nobody reads 5,000 accounts' posts anyway, and they overloaded the computers that held such users' timelines.

quiz.q: A job is timed with 8, 16, 32 and 64 workers. The work done rises and then falls: 64 workers do less than 32. Which part of the Universal Scalability Law must be above zero?
options: β, the cost of every pair of workers keeping in step
Only α, the time spent waiting for something only one worker can use
Neither: Amdahl's law already explains a fall
The speed of a single worker
quiz.why: With β = 0, the law becomes Amdahl's law, which flattens out but never falls. A fall means some cost grows with the number of pairs of workers, such as a step where every worker sends data to every other one, or a lock that wakes every waiting worker. The curve peaks at √((1 − α) / β) workers.

quiz.q: Aurora, Amazon's cloud database, runs the database program on one machine and keeps the data on a separate fleet of storage machines, with six copies of each piece. The database machine crashes in the middle of a busy minute. What happens to the payments it had already reported as saved?
options: They are lost, because the database machine's memory held them
They survive only if the database machine's own disk can be recovered
They are safe: a write counts as saved only once four of the six storage copies have its log record
They are undone, and the customers must pay again
quiz.why: Aurora keeps storage apart from compute. The database machine sends log records, short notes of each change, to the storage fleet, and reports a write as saved only once four of the six copies have it. A new database machine attaches to the same storage and carries on. The crashed machine's memory and disk held only a cache, which is the question to ask of every such system: where is the copy that lasts?

quiz.q: You want to page someone (send an alert that wakes them) when an incident has used 2% of the month's error budget within an hour. You don't want a page for short blips that use almost none, however many requests fail during them. The target is 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. Which rule does that?
options: Page when the last 10 minutes are below 99.9%
Page when more than 1% of requests fail for 5 minutes
Page when the burn rate is at least 14.4 over the last hour and over the last 5 minutes
Open a ticket when the burn rate is at least 1 over 3 days
quiz.why: A burn rate of 14.4 kept up for an hour spends 14.4 / 720 = 2% of a 30-day budget, since 30 days is 720 hours. Requiring the 5-minute window too makes the page stop soon after the fix. The 10-minute rule pages for blips that cost almost nothing. The 1%-for-5-minutes rule pages for a blip where 3% fail for 5 minutes, which uses only about 0.35% of the budget. The 3-day ticket is right for slow leaks, but it can't wake anyone within the hour.
